title: FCP Lab in CI

story: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, pushes a fix to its pull request for RH-1234, the "No projects yet" card. The unit tests are green in four minutes. Then the integration tests start, and the job says "Waiting for pending jobs". Two other pull requests are ahead of it, each holding the shared QA environment for its own run. Twenty-five minutes later Nova's run gets its turn, and fails: the test expects an empty workgroup, but a project from an earlier run is still there.
With people alone this queue was already annoying. With agents that push after every fix, it grows every week, and every run in it can be broken by the run before it.
hook.question: How can every pull request get a full copy of the product to test on, without waiting for anyone and without inheriting anyone else's data?

read.h: Why the shared environment needs a lock
p: fcp's integration tests run against QA, one real environment with one database. If two runs used it at the same time, each would change the other's data in the middle of a test. So the workflow takes a lock. In GitHub Actions the lock is a concurrency group: a name, and the rule that only one run with that name may run at a time while the others wait. The QA workflow's group is a fixed string, which means every pull request in the repo shares it.

The lock solves only half of the problem. It stops two runs from overlapping, but the second run still finds whatever the first one left behind. That is also why tests on QA came to depend on rows that someone created by hand years ago, as you saw in the lesson on builders. A shared environment remembers every run, and the lock turns it into a queue.

code.text:
# .github/workflows/_frontend-int-tests-reusable-aws.yml, as it is today
concurrency:
  group: frontend_integration_tests_aws
  cancel-in-progress: false

notes.text: A fixed name: every pull request's run lands in the same group, so they run one at a time.
false means a new run waits for the running one instead of stopping it.

read.h: A private copy of the product for every run
p: The other way round is to give every run its own environment and throw it away afterwards. People call this an ephemeral environment: it lives exactly as long as one run. FCP Lab is that for fcp. It boots the full product, the cloud, a real on-prem client (the Rhino software that normally runs inside a customer's network), the frontend and their databases, on one machine from a source tree, with fake seed data, so the workgroup in the story really is empty when the test starts.

In CI, each run boots its own Lab, named after the run (ci- plus the run's ID), on a runner of its own (the machine that runs one CI job), and nothing is shared with any other run. That is why the smoke workflow needs no lock. Its concurrency group has a different job: the name contains the branch, and cancel-in-progress is true, so when Nova pushes again, the older run of the same branch is stopped, because its result no longer matters. Two different pull requests never wait for each other.

code.text:
jobs:
  smoke:
    name: FCP Lab smoke
    runs-on: lab-runner-set
    concurrency:
      group: lab-smoke-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
      cancel-in-progress: true
    env:
      LAB_ID: ci-${{ github.run_id }}
    steps:
      - name: Boot the Lab from this commit's images
        run: python3 .lab/lab up --source "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE" --id "$LAB_ID" --mode snapshot --images "${{ inputs.image_tag }}"
      - name: Smoke suite
        run: python3 .lab/lab test "$LAB_ID" --suite core --json > core.json
      - name: Compare with main, only because something failed
        if: failure()
        run: python3 .lab/lab compare --source "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE" --id "cmp-$GITHUB_RUN_ID" --json > compare.json || true

notes.text: Runners that only run Labs. The deeper panel below says where they live.
One group per workflow and branch, not one for the whole repo.
A newer push on the same branch stops the older run. This is a way to save time, not a lock.
The Lab is named after this run, so two runs can never meet.
Boot from images that were already built for this commit; the next section explains them.
Comparing with main costs a second Lab, so it only runs when something failed.

deeper.h: Go deeper: where the Lab runs
p: A Lab is big for a CI job: it idles at about 3 GB of memory, grows during a test run, and its images take about 11 GB of disk. On the shared runners it would take memory and disk from every other job. So Labs get their own machines. Our runners live in the internal Kubernetes cluster as pods, Kubernetes' unit of one or more containers, and a tool called Karpenter adds and removes machines (nodes) as those pods need them. A NodePool tells Karpenter which kind of node to start, here 8 vCPU and 32 GB, at most six at a time.

A taint on those nodes keeps every other pod away: Kubernetes only places a pod there if it carries the matching toleration, and only the Lab runners do. Each runner asks for most of a node, so every Lab gets a machine to itself, and the Lab's containers run inside the runner pod through Docker-in-Docker: a second Docker engine that runs in its own container next to the runner, in the same pod. Before any of this, the Lab had to prove it runs on a clean Linux machine at all, because until then it had only been tested on Macs.

read.h: Build once per commit, boot many times
p: A Lab built from source takes ten minutes or more before the first test, which would eat most of a 15-minute budget. But the cloud, client and frontend workflows all run for the same commit, and later the comparison and the virtual machines our agents work in want the same Lab too. So the images are built once per commit, pushed to our container registry, and every later caller pulls them.

The trick is the tag, the name of one image version. Each image is tagged with the commit and the Lab's own version, because the Lab adds its own patches. Before building, the job asks the registry whether that tag exists, and if it does, it skips the build. One race is left: two workflows of the same commit can start at the same second, both find no tag and both build. A concurrency group named after the commit makes the second one wait, and when it runs, the tag is there. The registry also refuses to overwrite a tag, so an image can never change under a name that a test already used.

code.text:
concurrency: lab-images-${{ github.sha }}  # callers on one commit wait for each other
    steps:
      - name: Build and push once per commit
        run: |
          tag="${GITHUB_SHA}-lab$(python3 .lab/lab --version)"
          echo "tag=$tag" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          aws ecr describe-images --repository-name fcp-lab-cloud --image-ids imageTag="$tag" >/dev/null 2>&1 && exit 0
          python3 .lab/lab build --source "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE" --push "$REGISTRY/fcp-lab-{component}:$tag"

notes.text: No cancel-in-progress here: the second caller waits, then finds the tag.
The commit plus the Lab's version: one tag per source tree the Lab can boot.
The tag is already in the registry, so this caller is done.

p: A red smoke run raises one question before any other: did this pull request break it, or is main already broken? On QA people answered it by asking around. The smoke workflow answers it itself: only when something failed, it boots a second Lab from main's merge base, runs the same checks, and compares. The job summary then sorts every failure into regressed (red here, green on main), already failing on main, or suspect, where the comparison cannot say for sure and a person should look.

The smoke suite itself is short on purpose, so a run stays under about 15 minutes: the Lab's core proof, four to six fast frontend Playwright specs from e2e/pr/ picked by run time, and the contract suites that check the test fakes against the real client, object store and task queue. The long list of specs stays in the nightly run.

lab.title: A private stack per run, from an image built once
needs: About 60 MB for the node:24-alpine image
lab.goal: See two test runs break each other on one shared stack, then give every run a private copy named after the run, booted from an image that is built only once per commit.

guess.q: Run A and then run B use the same running stack. Each run checks that the workgroup is empty, adds one project and checks that there is exactly one. A finishes before B starts. What happens to B?

options.text: B passes, because the runs did not overlap.
options.why: A lock that stops overlap is not enough: A's project is still in the stack when B starts.

options.text: B fails at the first check, because the workgroup is no longer empty.
options.why: A shared environment remembers every run. B inherits A's project.

options.text: B waits until A's stack is reset.
options.why: Nothing resets a shared stack between runs unless someone builds that. It just keeps its data.

follow.say: Write a tiny stand-in for the product: an API that keeps projects in memory, a smoke test, an image for both, and a compose file. The smoke service is only started when you ask for it.
follow.see:
bb75c93 lab stack
(your commit id differs)

follow.say: Build the image for this commit with a script that skips the build when the tag already exists. Run it twice.
follow.do:
cat > images.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# Build the image for this commit once. Every later caller finds the tag and skips the build.
set -euo pipefail
tag=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
if docker image inspect "lab-api:$tag" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "lab-api:$tag already exists, skipping the build"
else
  docker build -q -t "lab-api:$tag" . >/dev/null && echo "built lab-api:$tag"
fi
EOF
chmod +x images.sh && ./images.sh && ./images.sh

lab.build: Write ci-run.sh, the shape of one CI run: it takes a run ID, calls ./images.sh (so only the first caller of a commit builds), boots a private stack named ci-<run id>, runs the smoke test, and always removes the stack at the end, also when the test fails (a trap on EXIT). Its exit code must be the smoke test's. Then start three runs at once with (./ci-run.sh 301 & ./ci-run.sh 302 & ./ci-run.sh 303 & wait) and check that all three pass, that the image was not built again, and that docker ps -a --filter name=ci- shows nothing afterwards.
checks: On the shared stack, the second smoke run fails because it finds the first run's project.
Two private stacks (-p ci-101 and -p ci-102) run at the same time and both pass.
./images.sh builds once per commit and prints "already exists, skipping the build" on the second call.
After a new commit, docker images lab-api lists two tags, one per commit.
Three ci-run.sh runs in parallel all pass, and docker ps -a --filter name=ci- is empty afterwards.

solution.text:
#!/bin/bash
# One CI run: the commit's image (built once), a private stack named after the run, the smoke test, and cleanup.
set -uo pipefail
run_id="${1:?usage: ./ci-run.sh <run id>}"
./images.sh
export TAG=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
trap 'docker compose -p "ci-$run_id" down >/dev/null 2>&1' EXIT
docker compose -p "ci-$run_id" run --rm -e RUN="$run_id" smoke 2>/dev/null

lab.fix: Someone wanted a short name in docker ps and added container_name: lab-api under the api service in compose.yaml. Add that line and start two private runs at the same time. One passes, the other fails with Conflict. The container name "/lab-api" is already in use. A fixed name is shared state again, just like the fixed QA lock: remove it so compose names each container after its project (ci-201-api-1, ci-202-api-1), and check that both runs pass.
explain: Why does the shared stack need a lock, and why does the lock still not make run B pass?
What is the difference between the QA workflow's concurrency group and the smoke workflow's, and why does only one of them cancel runs?
Two workflows of the same commit call ./images.sh at the same second. What can go wrong, and what does the concurrency group named after the commit change?
lab.done: Parallel runs on private stacks all pass, the image is built once per commit, and docker ps -a --filter name=ci- is empty when you finish.

check.q: The QA workflow's concurrency group is the fixed name frontend_integration_tests_aws. What does that mean for two pull requests that push at the same time?

options.text: They run at the same time, each on its own copy of QA.
options.why: There is only one QA. The group exists exactly because the runs cannot share it at the same time.

options.text: The second one waits until the first one is finished with QA.
options.why: A fixed group name is shared by every run in the repo, so they queue, one at a time.

options.text: The second one stops the first one.
options.why: That would need cancel-in-progress: true. The QA group sets false, so the newer run waits.

check.q: The smoke workflow's group is lab-smoke-<workflow>-<branch> with cancel-in-progress: true. Nova pushes twice in a minute. What happens?

options.text: The older run of that branch is stopped, and only the newest push is tested.
options.why: The older result no longer matters. Other branches have other group names, so they are not touched.

options.text: Both runs share one Lab to save money.
options.why: Every run boots its own Lab named after the run. Sharing would bring back the leftover data problem.

options.text: Every other pull request's smoke run is stopped too.
options.why: The branch is part of the name, so only runs of the same branch share the group.

check.q: A teammate suggests tagging the Lab's images latest instead of with the commit and the Lab's version. What goes wrong?

options.text: Nothing, as long as every run pulls the image right before it boots.
options.why: Pulling latest gives you whatever was pushed last, which may be another branch's commit. The run then tests code that is not in its pull request.

options.text: The registry refuses a tag called latest.
options.why: latest is a normal tag. The problem is what it means, not whether it is allowed.

options.text: One name now points at many versions over time, so a run can boot another commit's code and nobody can tell afterwards what was tested.
options.why: A tag per commit, which the registry never overwrites, means one name is one source tree, so every run tests exactly its own code.

p: First the Lab has to work on Linux: on a throw-away Ubuntu 24.04 m8i.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 32 GB, 100 GB gp3, no cloud credentials), ci/gate-d.sh wraps the Lab's ci/rehearse.sh, cold and warm, and records boot times, memory per service and docker system df, then repeats once inside a runner pod from ARC (Actions Runner Controller, which runs GitHub runners on Kubernetes) with Docker-in-Docker on inf-rhinohealth; the lab repo moves into the RhinoHealth org so CI can check it out with a GitHub App token. lab-runner-set is a new Karpenter NodePool fcp-lab (taint example.com/pool=fcp-lab:NoSchedule, cpu limit 48, a short consolidateAfter; decide spot or on-demand, since a Spot interruption makes a smoke run look flaky) in modules/karpenter-node-pool, and a scale set with min 0, max 6 runners (QA has 6 locks today), requests of 6 CPU, 24Gi and 80Gi, and a new optional runner_tolerations field in modules/github-runner-scale-sets; add the label to fcp's .github/actionlint.yaml.

_lab-images-reusable.yml pushes fcp-lab-cloud, -client and -frontend (tags_immutability_enabled) to ECR in the inf account, tagged <sha>-lab<lab version>, with concurrency lab-images-<sha>; add, with the Lab's owner, a lab command that builds and pushes a source tree's images and a way for lab up to pull them. _lab-smoke-reusable.yml runs lab test --suite core, the agreed pr/ specs and pytest tests_api -m contract --target lab inside the Lab's web-service, lab compare only on failure, and uploads the reports. Then frontend-ci moves pull requests to an e2e-lab job (suite frontend-e2e, the Lab's allowlist of 24 spec files) and keeps QA for main, the nightly and releases, with the e2e_tests alls-green gate moved into frontend-ci.yaml. Test it on a draft PR, never by dispatching frontend-ci on a branch, which deploys over main's dev dashboard and Storybook.

tickets.why: Prove the Lab on a clean Ubuntu VM and measure what it needs (Gate D).
lab-runner-set: the tainted Karpenter pool and the ARC scale set, one Lab per node.
Build the Lab's images once per commit, push them to ECR, skip when the tag exists.
The private smoke run on every PR, with lab compare only on failure: this lesson.
Move the frontend PR gate from qa-front-end to the Lab.

words.plain: One real environment, such as QA, that every run uses; it keeps the data each run leaves behind.
A name in a GitHub workflow; only one run with that name runs at a time.
With true, a new run in the group stops the running one; with false, it waits.
A private environment that lives for one run and is thrown away after it.
The name of one version of a container image; here the commit plus the Lab's version.
A Lab command that runs the same checks on main to say whether a failure is new.

review.q: Explain in three sentences why a lock on a shared environment is not enough, and what replaces it.
review.a: A lock stops runs from overlapping, so they queue, but each run still inherits the data the previous one left. A private environment per run, named after the run and thrown away after it, needs no lock and starts clean every time. The only group left is per branch, to stop an outdated run of the same branch.

review.q: Two workflows of one commit both ask for the Lab's images at the same moment. Describe what happens step by step.
review.a: The concurrency group named after the commit lets the first one run while the second waits. The first finds no tag, builds and pushes. The second then runs, finds the tag in the registry and skips the build.

review.q: The smoke run is red. What does lab compare tell you, and why does it only run on failure?
review.a: It runs the same checks on main and sorts each failure into regressed, already failing on main, or suspect. It needs a second Lab, so a green run skips it.

remember: Give every run its own throw-away copy of the product, named after the run and booted from images built once per commit: no lock, no queue, no leftovers.
